newsitem.title: FRANCE: Delors raps German drive for EU stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Delors raps German drive for EU stability pact.

text.p: Former European Commission President Jacques Delors voiced grave doubts on Thursday about Germany's drive for a "stability pact" to enforce strict budget discipline after the creation of a single European currency.

Delors, who headed the Commission from 1985 to 1995, told a news conference that economic and monetary union (EMU) must not be reduced to a question of a single currency and budget discipline, otherwise the public would reject it.
The EU needed an "economic government" to boost growth and employment and balance out the monetary discipline imposed by an independent European central bank, the French socialist said.
"Like (Commission president) Jacques Santer, I am in favour of a pact for growth and solidarity rather than (a stability pact)," he said.

Germany on Monday demanded stiff fines for countries that fail to limit budget deficits after the start of EMU. It has also been insisting on the strictest interpretation of the criteria for joining the planned single currency in 1999.
But Delors warned that could lead to a clash.
"I think there is a risk that Germany will exasperate its partners. Not all of them, but some," he said.

"We have to get away from the idea that the tougher we are on the criteria, the more we will reassure the Germans, who are worried about giving up the mark. This is bound to lead us to a confrontation," Delors said.

"If someone is trying to impose on us an economic and monetary union in which the word 'economic' is struck out and 'monetary union' is reduced to a single currency and budget discipline, I say no. That is not what we agreed to in the Maastricht treaty," he said of the EMU treaty.

Delors' criticism of the stability pact put him at odds with France's conservative government, which has backed Bonn on the plan. Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday it was a guarantee that members of the single currency would not adopt budgetary policies that caused high interest rates or endanger the strength of the euro.

Delors said the 1992 treaty, of which he was one of the main architects, was carefully drafted to leave the necessary leeway for a political decision on which countries qualify for EMU, and the current debate on the criteria was pointless and damaging.
"Public debate about who will be in (the first wave of EMU) only complicates the situation...and will only aggravate the malaise in Germany and the Netherlands," he said.
He said European political leaders should keep quiet and allow countries such as Italy, Spain and Portugal to make courageous efforts to meet the conditions.
"We shouldn't slam the door on anyone today or substitute for their governments," he said.
Delors said it was good that former chancellor Helmut Schmidt had triggered debate in Germany over the dangers of excessive insistence on budget discipline.
Schmidt warned the Bonn government and the Bundesbank last week that they were isolating Germany and putting an ugly face on its EU policies by harping on strict fiscal rigour.

Delors also said it was legitimate to discuss the future exchange rate between the euro, the future single currency, and the dollar and wrong to say it should simply be left to the financial markets to decide.
By pursuing a more active policy to promote growth and jobs, the EU would naturally bring the euro rate closer to a realistic level against the dollar, which was undervalued, he said.
The news conference was to launch a book of his 1992-95 speeches on European policy entitled "Combats pour l'Europe"
(Battles for Europe).
